name: Shamrock
lede: Shamrock is the bright green of Ireland's clover-like emblem, and the story of how green replaced blue as the Irish color is more tangled than it looks.

sections.title: Before green, a blue
sections.body:
St Clair tells the tale this way: St Patrick, a Briton captured and brought to Ireland as a slave, escaped, returned as a missionary and is most famously said to have used a shamrock to explain the Trinity [1]. By the seventh century he was celebrated as a saint, having died late in the fifth [1]. Yet until the middle of the eighteenth century the color most associated with him was a shade of blue [1].

The shift from St Patrick's blue to green was convoluted [1]. St Clair says Irish Catholics, reacting to the hostility they saw in William of Orange and his orange-wearing Protestant supporters, wanted a symbolic color of their own [1]. The shamrock had by then become central to Irish Catholic identity, and green had become associated with revolution after Camille Desmoulins stuck a linden leaf in his hat on 12 July 1789 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a vivid screen green, much more saturated than a real clover leaf [2]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, no work holds a color within six units of it across five per cent of the canvas [2]. Paintings do not use this green at that scale, so it is not a museum-canvas color [2].
